title: Connections between cube dissection impossibility and packing problems

problemStatement.formal: ∀ p : CubePacking, p.allDifferentSizes → p.cubes.Nonempty → p.totalVolume < 1 ∨ ¬(∃ d : CubeDissection, d.toPacking = p)
problemStatement.plain: What are the connections between the impossibility of dissecting a cube into cubes of all different sizes and packing problems?
whyMatters: Bridges impossibility theorem with quantitative packing bounds
Shows dimension contrast: 2D allows squared squares, 3D does not
Connects to de Bruijn's classical brick tiling theorem

proven: Size properties transfer between dissection and packing
No distinct-size packing achieves volume fraction 1 (dissection-packing bridge)
Reciprocal packings (side lengths 1/n) have distinct sizes
open: Supremum of achievable volume fractions for distinct-size cube packings
Optimal packing of cubes of sizes 1,2,...,n into smallest container
knownResults.goal: Formalize structural connections between dissection and packing

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED: Formalized connections between cube dissection impossibility and packing problems. Key theorem: no packing of distinct-size cubes achieves volume 1.
insights: The dissection impossibility directly constrains packing: distinct-size packings cannot achieve volume fraction 1
2D is special: squared squares exist, so the 2D dissection-packing connection is fundamentally different
The infinite descent argument generalizes to all dimensions n≥3
de Bruijn's theorem provides an algebraic criterion for brick tilings that contrasts with the distinct-size problem
Volume bounds alone don't explain the impossibility — the topological structure of the floor covering is key
mathlibGaps: Measure theory needed for rigorous volume bound proof (Lebesgue measure on packing)

approaches.name: Packing-dissection bridge
approaches.description: Define packing as relaxation of dissection, prove that dissection impossibility implies packing density < 1 for distinct sizes.

papers: de Bruijn (1969) - Filling boxes with bricks
Duijvestijn (1978) - Simple perfect squared square of lowest order
